title: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate · Units 73–74
description: Curated compound nouns and word partners, with spelling, stress, semantic contrasts and reviewed exercise vocabulary.

units.title: Unit 73 — Compound nouns
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 152–153 (PDF pages 153–154).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Recognise compound nouns for people, places, transport, objects, money and everyday activities.
Choose the correct spelling of compounds written as one word, two words or with a hyphen.
Notice variable stress patterns, including haircut and income tax versus public transport and full stop.
Form new compounds by reusing a component such as hair, bus, card or air.
Practise compound nouns introduced or revisited in exercises 73.1–73.4.

items.example: We watched an ice hockey match on Saturday.
items.note: An ice sport played with sticks and a puck; normally two written words.

items.example: Public transport is often cheaper than driving to work.
items.note: Buses, trains and other services available to everyone; the main stress is on transport.

items.example: We found a quiet campsite near the lake.
items.note: An area where people can pitch tents or park caravans; written as one word.

items.pt: babá; pessoa que cuida de crianças por algumas horas
items.example: We hired a babysitter for Friday evening.
items.note: A person paid to look after children while their parents are away.

items.example: Income tax is taken from part of her salary.
items.note: Tax paid on income; the first word carries the main stress.

items.example: Spanish is his mother tongue, but he also speaks English.
items.note: The first language learned in childhood; not necessarily the language currently spoken most.

items.example: Our travel agent booked the flights and hotel together.
items.note: Someone who makes travel arrangements for customers.

items.pt: cineasta; produtor ou realizador de filmes
items.example: The film-maker spent months interviewing local people.
items.note: A person who makes films; this textbook writes the compound with a hyphen.

items.example: Finish each statement with a full stop.
items.note: British English term for the punctuation mark at the end of a statement; main stress on stop.

items.example: I need a haircut before the wedding.
items.note: The act or style of cutting hair; compound with main stress on hair.

items.example: The hairdresser cut and styled her hair.
items.note: A person whose job is to cut and style hair.

items.example: The hairdryer stopped working while I was getting ready.
items.note: Electrical appliance for drying hair; also written hair dryer in some varieties.

items.example: The museum has a ramp for wheelchair users.
items.note: A chair with wheels used by people who cannot walk or have difficulty walking.

items.example: There is a new tube of toothpaste in the bathroom.
items.note: Substance used with a toothbrush to clean teeth.

items.example: Remember to pack your toothbrush for the trip.
items.note: Small brush used to clean your teeth.

items.example: She keeps her socks in the top drawer of the chest of drawers.
items.note: Piece of furniture with several drawers, usually used for storing clothes.

items.example: The DJ played music until two in the morning.
items.note: Short for disc jockey; someone who plays recorded music on the radio or at events.

items.example: The disc jockey introduced the next song on the radio.
items.note: Full form of DJ; the two forms refer to the same role.

items.example: Take your sunglasses because it will be bright outside.
items.note: Always plural in this meaning; say a pair of sunglasses.

items.example: Turn right at the crossroads after the petrol station.
items.note: Place where two roads cross; it ends in -s even when referring to one junction.

items.example: I stopped at a cashpoint to withdraw some money.
items.note: British English term for an ATM; written as one word.

items.example: Wait until the traffic lights turn green.
items.note: Road signals that control when drivers and pedestrians can move.

items.example: She wore silver earrings to the celebration.
items.note: Jewellery worn in the ears; often used in the plural.

items.example: He wore a plain white T-shirt under his jacket.
items.note: Common compound written with a hyphen and capital T.

items.example: You can pay by credit card at the ticket office.
items.note: Card used to buy goods or services with credit; two written words.

items.example: The nearest bus stop is opposite the library.
items.note: A place where buses pick up or drop off passengers; two words.

items.example: We arrived at the airport two hours early.
items.note: One-word compound from air and port; compare airline and aircraft.

items.example: Which airline are you flying with?
items.note: Company that operates passenger or cargo flights.

items.example: Several aircraft were waiting to take off.
items.note: Aircraft has the same form in the singular and plural.

items.example: The bus driver waited for the last passenger.
items.note: A person who drives a bus; compare bus stop and bus station.

items.example: We met outside the bus station in the town centre.
items.note: A place where buses arrive and leave, often with several stops.

items.pt: carteira de identidade; documento de identificação
items.example: Please show your ID card at the entrance.
items.note: ID stands for identity; an ID card establishes who someone is.

items.pt: carteira de identidade; documento de identidade
items.example: She took her identity card when she registered.
items.note: Long form of ID card; a card giving information about a person.

items.example: I sent my grandmother a birthday card.
items.note: A card with a birthday message; compare credit card and ID card.

items.example: We usually eat dinner together in the dining room.
items.note: An additional room compound used in the exercise answer key.

items.example: My sister-in-law lives in Manchester.
items.note: A spouse’s sister or a sibling’s wife; hyphens are standard.

items.example: His mother-in-law is staying for the weekend.
items.note: Mother of your spouse; plural: mothers-in-law.

items.example: I invited my father-in-law to lunch.
items.note: Father of your spouse; plural: fathers-in-law.

items.example: She returned from her holiday with a suntan.
items.note: A darker skin colour caused by the sun; avoid confusing this with sunburn.

items.example: We sat outside and enjoyed the afternoon sunshine.
items.note: Natural light from the sun.

items.example: Use sunblock when you spend time outdoors.
items.note: A product that protects the skin from sunlight; sunscreen is also common.

items.example: He got sunburn after a day at the beach.
items.note: Skin damage caused by too much sunlight.

items.example: Remember to put on sunscreen before you go out.
items.note: Lotion or cream that helps protect skin from the sun.

items.example: We missed the start of the film because of a traffic jam.
items.note: Many vehicles moving very slowly or not moving on a road.

items.example: She sat in an armchair and read a book.
items.note: A comfortable chair with supports for the arms.

items.pt: diretor de cinema; diretora de cinema
items.example: The film director explained the scene to the actors.
items.note: Person directing how a film is made; related to film-maker.

sectionsChecked: A: Formation and pictured compound nouns
B: One word or two?; T-shirt, credit card and bus stop
C: Pronunciation and changing compound stress
D: Forming new compounds: air-, bus- and -card families
Exercises 73.1–73.4 and answer key on PDF page 236

units.title: Unit 74 — Word partners
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 154–155 (PDF pages 155–156).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Recognise that natural English uses conventional word partners, also called collocations.
Use common verb–noun combinations such as make a mistake, miss the bus and score a goal.
Select adjective–noun combinations for number, amount, choice, vocabulary, noise and traffic.
Use common adverb–adjective pairs such as terribly sorry, vitally important, fast asleep and wide awake.
Avoid non-standard combinations illustrated in exercises 74.1–74.4 and apply contrasts from the answer key.

items.pt: palavra que costuma acompanhar outra; colocação
items.example: A good dictionary can help you learn the word partners of a noun.
items.note: A word that commonly occurs with another word; often called a collocation.

items.example: Heavy traffic is a common English collocation.
items.note: Two or more words that are conventionally used together.

items.example: We spent time exploring the old town.
items.note: Use spend time, not pass time, for time spent in a place or activity.

items.example: I missed the bus and had to walk home.
items.note: Miss a bus, train or flight means fail to catch it; not lose the bus.

items.example: They would like to have children in the future.
items.note: Use have children when talking about becoming or being parents.

items.example: I made a mistake when I copied the address.
items.note: Use make, not do, with mistake.

items.pt: um ferimento grave; uma lesão grave
items.example: She suffered a serious injury during the match.
items.note: Serious is natural with injury; grave injury is not the taught everyday pairing.

items.example: His aunt is recovering from a serious illness.
items.note: Serious is also a natural partner of illness.

items.example: It is quite likely that the shop will close early.
items.note: Quite likely means fairly probable; followed by that + clause in this example.

items.example: The cost will depend on the number of guests.
items.note: The preposition is on, not of; depend on someone or something.

items.example: My cousin told me a joke about a talking cat.
items.note: Tell someone a joke; do not say said me a joke.

items.example: He wants to lose weight by exercising regularly.
items.note: The opposite is put on weight. Lose and loose are different words.

items.example: I tend to put on weight when I stop exercising.
items.note: Opposite of lose weight; put on is a phrasal verb.

items.example: She decided to go on a diet before the summer.
items.note: Start following a plan to change what you eat, often to lose weight.

items.example: No one can predict the future with complete certainty.
items.note: Predict means say what may happen before it happens.

items.pt: ganhar um jogo; vencer uma partida
items.example: Our team hopes to win the game on Sunday.
items.note: Use win a game or match for a result; beat an opposing team or person.

items.example: She scored a goal in the final minute.
items.note: In football and similar sports, score a goal means get a point by sending the ball into the goal.

items.pt: um alarme dispara; um alarme toca
items.example: The security alarm goes off whenever the back door opens.
items.note: Go off can mean start making a loud warning sound, not stop working in this sense.

items.example: They fell in love while studying at university.
items.note: Past form: fell in love; often followed by with someone.

items.example: They plan to get married next spring.
items.note: An event or change in status; be married describes the state.

items.pt: estar esperando um bebê; estar grávida
items.example: Maya and Oliver are expecting a baby in December.
items.note: Be expecting a baby indicates a pregnancy; do not use waiting for a baby for this meaning.

items.pt: ter um bebê; dar à luz
items.example: Their neighbours had a baby last week.
items.note: Use had a baby when referring to the birth; an exercise contrast with got a baby.

items.example: A large number of visitors arrived before noon.
items.note: Use number with countable plural nouns such as people or books.

items.example: A small number of students missed the class.
items.note: Opposite of a large number of; use with countable plural nouns.

items.example: A limited number of tickets are still available.
items.note: Emphasises a restriction on the number of countable things.

items.example: Repairing the roof will cost a large amount of money.
items.note: Use amount with uncountable nouns such as money; not a big amount of money.

items.pt: uma grande variedade de; ampla escolha de
items.example: The café offers a wide choice of sandwiches.
items.note: A large range of possibilities; contrast a limited or narrow choice.

items.pt: uma variedade restrita de; poucas opções de
items.example: The small shop has a narrow choice of winter coats.
items.note: Opposite of a wide choice; fewer options available.

items.pt: uma variedade limitada de; poucas opções de
items.example: There is a limited choice of vegetarian meals.
items.note: A conventional opposite to a wide choice.

items.example: Reading novels has helped her develop a wide vocabulary.
items.note: Wide describes a rich range of words known or used by someone.

items.example: At first, I could communicate with only a limited vocabulary.
items.note: Opposite of a wide vocabulary; avoid little vocabulary in the exercise context.

items.pt: um barulho alto; um ruído forte
items.example: We heard a loud noise coming from upstairs.
items.note: Use loud, not big, for the volume of a noise.

items.example: Good communication is of great importance to the team.
items.note: Formal construction meaning very important; great, not big, is the taught partner.

items.example: The boat trip was great fun for everyone.
items.note: Informal positive evaluation: an experience was very enjoyable.

items.example: There was heavy traffic on the road into town.
items.note: Many vehicles causing busy or slow roads; the opposite is light traffic.

items.example: We travelled early when there was light traffic.
items.note: The natural opposite of heavy traffic.

items.example: I am terribly sorry about the misunderstanding.
items.note: Intensifying adverb before sorry; a strong, polite apology.

items.example: We are well aware of the risks involved.
items.note: Well aware of something means fully conscious or informed about it.

items.example: It is vitally important to check the brakes before travelling.
items.note: Very important; vitally is not interchangeable with every adjective.

items.example: The children were fast asleep when we came home.
items.note: Completely asleep, not asleep quickly; fast functions as an intensifier here.

items.example: It was midnight, but she was still wide awake.
items.note: Fully awake; natural contrast with fast asleep.

sectionsChecked: A: Word partners and frequent errors; language-help box
B: Verbs and nouns, including illustrations for goal, alarm and expecting a baby
C: Adjectives and nouns; scale and opposite combinations
D: Adverbs and adjectives; intensity and completion
Exercises 74.1–74.5 and answer key on PDF page 237
